name: Sample Social Systems Knowledge Corpus
description: A small, curated demonstration corpus about cooperation, common-pool resources, social networks and collective-action problems. Summaries are original short paraphrases for retrieval practice, not substitutes for the cited works.

documents.title: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action
documents.content: Elinor Ostrom examines common-pool resource governance using empirical cases of collective action. The work challenges the assumption that shared resources can only be governed through a single universal solution such as central state control or privatization. It is relevant to theories about resource users, locally developed rules, collective choice, monitoring, institutional diversity and self-organized governance. The conditions found in particular cases matter; this record does not imply that every community-managed resource succeeds.

documents.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
documents.content: Robert Axelrod studies how cooperation can emerge among self-interested actors through repeated interactions, including the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. The work is useful when a theory proposes reciprocity, repeated exchange, strategic adaptation, incentives or cooperation without a central authority. Its results depend on the interaction structure and assumptions; they should not be generalized to every social setting without examination.

documents.title: The Strength of Weak Ties
documents.content: Mark Granovetter's article develops the idea that weaker interpersonal ties can connect otherwise separated social circles and help explain the movement of information and influence across groups. It is relevant when a proposed theory includes networks, relationships of differing strengths, diffusion, bridging connections or community organization. A network analogy should preserve the differences between the proposed relationships and the article's sociological setting.

documents.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
documents.content: Garrett Hardin's 1968 article frames a collective-action problem around shared resources and competing individual incentives. It is a historically influential perspective for examining resource pressure, open access, incentives and possible overuse. It should be considered alongside empirical and institutional work on cases where communities develop arrangements to govern shared resources; the article is not a universal law for every commons.
